examples.original_efsa_comment:
Plant products: The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU levels are identical. In the framework of the renewal of the approval for cyprodinil, a new residue definition for risk assessment for fruit crops is under discussion (Cyprodinil and CGA232449 (free and conjugated)). In addition, a residue definition for rotational crops is under discussion (NOA422054 (free and conjugate)).
Animal products: In contrast to the JMPR, the EU residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment include metabolite CGA304075 in either free (animal tissues) or in free and conjugated form (milk). However, as Codex MRLs are not proposed for commodities of animal origin, these differences in residue definitions are of low importance.

examples.original_efsa_comment:
Considering that clothianidin and thiamethoxam have different toxicological reference values, at EU level the residue definitions for plant products and products from ruminants and pigs were derived as clothianidin and thiamethoxam separately. Since also JMPR derived separated Codex MRL proposals for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, these residue definitions can be considered comparable with the definitions derived by the JMPR.
No residue definition was derived for poultry products during the MRL review since poultry were not expected to be exposed to significant residues of clothianidin or thiamethoxam. Nevertheless, in the reasoned opinion on the MRL review, EFSA considered the residue definitions proposed by JMPR consistent with the findings of the metabolism studies available (EFSA, 2014r). This conclusion is still considered valid.

examples.original_efsa_comment:
Fipronil sulfone metabolite (MB46136) Fipronil desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513) Fipronil sulfide metabolite (MB45950) The enforcement residue definitions derived by the JMPR and the EU peer review/MRL review are comparable. The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR is wider than the EU risk assessment residue definition. It includes the sum of fipronil, the desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513), the sulfone metabolite (MB46136) and the sulfide metabolite (MB45950).
New metabolism studies, investigating the metabolic pathway of fipronil following foliar treatments were evaluated by the JMPR 2021 (cabbage potato, rice, cotton, sunflower) which have not been available for the EU assessments. These studies, however, were not the reason to amend the residue definition for risk assessment as derived by the JMPR in 2002. The studies confirmed the presence of photometabolite of fipronil (desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513)) following foliar treatment.
The sulfide metabolite (MB45950), also included in the risk assessment residue definitions, was present in rice straw (9.3–16.8%) following seed/foliar treatment, but generally not detected or present at low levels in other commodities. The sulfide metabolite (MB45950) was present also in goat matrices (up to 12% TRR).
Overall, the JMPR concluded that metabolites MB46513 and MB45950 could make a significant contribution to the overall consumer exposure when compared with estimates for the sum of fipronil and fipronil-sulfone and therefore included these compounds in the risk assessment residue definition. The EU pesticides peer review derived the risk assessment and enforcement residue definitions for the representative use, i.e.
seed treatment; the photodegradation product of fipronil-desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513) was not included in the residue definitions as unlikely to occur in seed treatments or soil incorporation. However, because of concern that the desulfinyl metabolite forms as a result of photodegradation, it was proposed that treated seed must be kept in the dark prior to use. The MRL review confirmed the residue definitions derived by the EU pesticides peer review.
The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR is adequate to account for the potential metabolites of fipronil in plant commodities (from seed/soil and foliar applications) and in animal matrices. The exposure assessment performed according to this residue definition is expected to be protective for consumers. The JMPR also evaluated hydrolysis studies submitted to investigate the effect of processing on the nature of fipronil, MB46136 and MB46153.
Fipronil under sterilisation conditions slightly degraded for 5.5% AR to fipronil-amide (toxicity covered by fipronil). Fipronil sulfone (MB46136) also degraded under sterilisation conditions only and for 8.4% AR to RPA105320 (fipronil-sulfone-amide). Fipronil-desulfinyl was the most unstable and under sterilisation conditions formed two major degradation products: MB46400 (10.5% AR) and fipronil-carboxamide (25.9% AR; RPA105048).
For the estimation of consumer exposure to these degradation products the JMPR proposed to apply the TTC (Cramer Class III threshold of 1.5 μg/kg bw per day).

examples.original_efsa_comment: The EU and JMPR enforcement residue definitions for plants are nearly identical, covering only parent fenazaquin. In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected. For animals there is a slight difference in the residue definition for enforcement and RA, since EFSA is proposing fenazaquin only (for ruminants), while JMPR proposes a wider RD which includes also metabolites, i.e. tautomeric forms of 4‐hydroxyquinazoline (only for risk assessment) and 2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (for enforcement and risk assessment). The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS. The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.

In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected. For animals there is a slight difference in the residue definition for enforcement and RA, since EFSA is proposing fenazaquin only (for ruminants), while JMPR proposes a wider RD which includes also metabolites, i.e. tautomeric forms of 4‐hydroxyquinazoline (only for risk assessment) and 2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (for enforcement and risk assessment). The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS. The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.
examples.rationale: EFSA describes the plant enforcement definitions as nearly identical because both cover parent fenazaquin alone. It nevertheless notes that EU plant definitions are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR has a global enforcement definition, so comparability does not establish equal crop coverage.

For the commodity under discussion in this CCPR meeting (i.e. tea), the EU and Codex enforcement and risk assessment residue definitions are identical. However, in the EU, an additional residue definition was established, encompassing 4‐chloroaniline (PCA) a genotoxic carcinogen metabolite (EFSA). At EU level no metabolism studies are available for leafy crops to cover the Codex MRL proposal for tea
In the EU, standard hydrolysis studies with radiolabelled diflubenzuron were available to investigate the degradation of residues under conditions simulating pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation. Significant degradation of diflubenzuron occurred under sterilisation conditions (pH of 6, temperature 120°C), leading to the formation of PCA up to 58% of the applied radioactivity (AR), and the detection of 4‐chlorophenylurea (CPU) at 6%, a precursor of PCA
Tea is primarily consumed as an infusion prepared from fermented/dried tea leaves with boiling water. Information on the formation of PCA during fermentation/drying is not available. The pH of tea infusions is neutral/slightly acidic; for green tea infusions. In standard hydrolysis studies, the formation of PCA was not observed under boiling conditions (pH 5, 100°C), EFSA is of the opinion that the available data do not allow to exclude the presence of PCA in tea infusion (100°C, neutral or slightly acidic pH)
The transfer of diflubenzuron residues from tea leaves into tea infusions was assessed by JMPR. In this study, the possible formation of PCA was not investigated

Peer review (EFSA, 2015e): (1) Diflubenzuron and 4‐chlorophenylurea (CPU), expressed as diflubenzuron (2) PCA and provisionally PCAA, expressed as PCA (pending full assessment of toxicological properties of PCAA)

At EU level, metabolism studies were available for fruits and mushrooms; JMPR had studies available for maize, soybean, apple, cabbage, cotton, orange, mushrooms, rice, wheat and beans, which were assessed in its previous assessments (JMPR 2002, 2011). For the current assessment, no new metabolism studies were reported It would be desirable that JMPR in its assessment discusses the relevance of the metabolism studies and the appropriateness of the current residue definitions for the new uses assessed For the commodity under discussion in this CCPR meeting (i.e. tea), the EU and Codex enforcement and risk assessment residue definitions are identical. However, in the EU, an additional residue definition was established, encompassing 4‐chloroaniline (PCA) a genotoxic carcinogen metabolite (EFSA). At EU level no metabolism studies are available for leafy crops to cover the Codex MRL proposal for tea

In the EU, standard hydrolysis studies with radiolabelled diflubenzuron were available to investigate the degradation of residues under conditions simulating pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation. Significant degradation of diflubenzuron occurred under sterilisation conditions (pH of 6, temperature 120°C), leading to the formation of PCA up to 58% of the applied radioactivity (AR), and the detection of 4‐chlorophenylurea (CPU) at 6%, a precursor of PCA Tea is primarily consumed as an infusion prepared from fermented/dried tea leaves with boiling water. Information on the formation of PCA during fermentation/drying is not available. The pH of tea infusions is neutral/slightly acidic; for green tea infusions. In standard hydrolysis studies, the formation of PCA was not observed under boiling conditions (pH 5, 100°C), EFSA is of the opinion that the available data do not allow to exclude the presence of PCA in tea infusion (100°C, neutral or slightly acidic pH) The transfer of diflubenzuron residues from tea leaves into tea infusions was assessed by JMPR. In this study, the possible formation of PCA was not investigated
examples.rationale: EFSA notes an additional EU definition for PCA and missing leafy-crop metabolism data. The same comment describes the tea definitions as identical, so it is qualified context for the broader difference, not an unqualified statement that every plant definition differs.
examples.rationale_ko: EFSA는 EU의 추가 PCA 정의와 잎채소 대사자료 부족을 언급한다. 같은 코멘트는 차의 정의가 동일하다고도 하므로 모든 식물 정의가 다르다는 단정으로 요약하지 않는다.
examples.note: No와 단순 일치하는 문장만 골라 쓰지 않는다. 차(tea)에 대한 동일성 진술과 추가 PCA 정의를 함께 보존한다.

examples.original_efsa_comment: Plant commodities: Metabolism of cyflumetofen was investigated in fruit crops (mandarin, apple and eggplant) at EU and JMPR level (JMPR 2014). Cyflumetofen constituted the major portion of total radioactive residue (TRR), ranging from 67% to 84% TRR initially and 44%–65% TRR after 30 days on fruits, and 77%–87% TRR initially and 44%–81% TRR after 30 days on leaves. Among identified metabolites, only 2‐(trifluoromethyl) benzoic acid (metabolite B‐1) (free and conjugated), exceeded 10% TRR (up to 15% and 16% TRR, free and conjugated, respectively, in eggplant fruits), and AB‐6 at 10% TRR in eggplant leaves The current residue definitions at EU and JMPR levels are similar During EU MRL review, the lack of metabolism studies in leafy crops was considered acceptable only for hops, assuming that the metabolic pattern is similar to eggplant leaves at 14 PHI and field trials on hops. However, it was highlighted that a metabolism study on leafy would be desirable to confirm this assumption Under the current evaluation, JMPR received new GAPs for hops, tea and coffee beans. As JMPR noted that no metabolism studies exist for leafy crops and pulses/oilseeds, essential for hops, tea and coffee beans uses, JMPR re‐evaluated the metabolism studies submitted in 2014. JMPR concluded that the metabolism observed in apple and mandarin tree leaves can be considered representative for tea leaves, as both are permanent woody crops. Metabolism in hops was found to be sufficiently addressed by the metabolism studies in eggplants (leaves), mandarin and apple tree leaves. For coffee beans, JMPR considered the metabolism studies in fruit being sufficiently representative, as coffee berries are categorised as fruits Overall, the previously derived residue definitions were confirmed for the additional commodities under assessment The approach used by JMPR to extrapolate the results of metabolism studies in fruit crops to coffee beans is not fully in line with the EU practices and with the requirements described in the FAO manual. Risk management discussion is therefore recommended to decide whether the approach is acceptable Processed commodities: In standard hydrolysis studies, cyflumetofen was found to degrade to B‐1 (44–75% AR) and AB‐1 (32–49% AR) under boiling/brewing and sterilisation conditions These findings suggest that the setting of a separate residue definition for processed products should be considered, as previously suggested in the MRL review (EFSA, 2021f) Animal commodities: The RDs for enforcement derived by JMPR and at EU level are different: At EU level, it was therefore decided not to include metabolite B‐1 in the enforcement residue definition for animal products, since this metabolite is not specific for cyflumetofen (it can be also formed from flutolanil and fluopyram and any of their metabolites containing the 2‐trifluoromethylbenzyl moiety)

Plant commodities: Metabolism of cyflumetofen was investigated in fruit crops (mandarin, apple and eggplant) at EU and JMPR level (JMPR 2014). Cyflumetofen constituted the major portion of total radioactive residue (TRR), ranging from 67% to 84% TRR initially and 44%–65% TRR after 30 days on fruits, and 77%–87% TRR initially and 44%–81% TRR after 30 days on leaves. Among identified metabolites, only 2‐(trifluoromethyl) benzoic acid (metabolite B‐1) (free and conjugated), exceeded 10% TRR (up to 15% and 16% TRR, free and conjugated, respectively, in eggplant fruits), and AB‐6 at 10% TRR in eggplant leaves
The current residue definitions at EU and JMPR levels are similar
During EU MRL review, the lack of metabolism studies in leafy crops was considered acceptable only for hops, assuming that the metabolic pattern is similar to eggplant leaves at 14 PHI and field trials on hops. However, it was highlighted that a metabolism study on leafy would be desirable to confirm this assumption
Under the current evaluation, JMPR received new GAPs for hops, tea and coffee beans. As JMPR noted that no metabolism studies exist for leafy crops and pulses/oilseeds, essential for hops, tea and coffee beans uses, JMPR re‐evaluated the metabolism studies submitted in 2014. JMPR concluded that the metabolism observed in apple and mandarin tree leaves can be considered representative for tea leaves, as both are permanent woody crops. Metabolism in hops was found to be sufficiently addressed by the metabolism studies in eggplants (leaves), mandarin and apple tree leaves. For coffee beans, JMPR considered the metabolism studies in fruit being sufficiently representative, as coffee berries are categorised as fruits
Overall, the previously derived residue definitions were confirmed for the additional commodities under assessment
The approach used by JMPR to extrapolate the results of metabolism studies in fruit crops to coffee beans is not fully in line with the EU practices and with the requirements described in the FAO manual. Risk management discussion is therefore recommended to decide whether the approach is acceptable
Processed commodities: In standard hydrolysis studies, cyflumetofen was found to degrade to B‐1 (44–75% AR) and AB‐1 (32–49% AR) under boiling/brewing and sterilisation conditions
These findings suggest that the setting of a separate residue definition for processed products should be considered, as previously suggested in the MRL review (EFSA, 2021f)
Animal commodities: The RDs for enforcement derived by JMPR and at EU level are different: At EU level, it was therefore decided not to include metabolite B‐1 in the enforcement residue definition for animal products, since this metabolite is not specific for cyflumetofen (it can be also formed from flutolanil and fluopyram and any of their metabolites containing the 2‐trifluoromethylbenzyl moiety)
